items.stem: In Lean, 'waiting' is considered a waste because it:

options.text: Consumes time and resources without adding customer value
options.rationale: Correct: waiting is non-value-adding time the customer would not pay for.

options.text: Always requires more staff to fix
options.rationale: Waiting is a waste regardless of staffing changes.

options.text: Is the only true form of waste
options.rationale: It is one of several wastes, not the only one.

options.text: Adds value by letting work rest

items.explanation: Correct: waiting is non-value-adding time the customer would not pay for.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO are true about takt time? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It is set by customer demand over available working time
options.rationale: Correct: takt = available time / demand, the pace of customer need.

options.text: Producing faster than takt builds excess inventory
options.rationale: Correct: outpacing takt creates overproduction waste.

options.text: Takt time is the time a machine takes to cycle
options.rationale: That is cycle time, not takt time.

options.text: Takt time increases when demand increases
options.rationale: Higher demand lowers takt time, speeding the required pace.

items.explanation: Correct: takt = available time / demand, the pace of customer need.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: In Lean thinking, value is defined by:

options.text: The customer, in terms of what they are willing to pay for
options.rationale: Correct: Lean defines value from the customer's perspective.
Cost targets are internal, not the definition of value.

options.text: The number of process steps performed
options.rationale: More steps do not mean more value.

options.text: The size of the production batch
options.rationale: Batch size is unrelated to customer value.

items.explanation: Correct: Lean defines value from the customer's perspective.
